messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aroha Tane is a 63-year-old Māori woman, married and working as a project manager for a regional infrastructure firm in Auckland-adjacent New Zealand before relocating with her husband to the Pacific Northwest of the United States several years ago. She presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 62, describing a clinical picture that has progressively narrowed her world since a life-threatening illness eighteen months prior.

The precipitating event occurred during what Aroha had initially dismissed as fatigue and mild chest tightness. She collapsed at her desk during a site planning call, and was rushed to hospital, where she spent eleven days in intensive care following a severe cardiac event complicated by sepsis. She remembers, with a clarity that horrifies her, the sensation of being intubated — the cold metal of the laryngoscope, the pressure against her throat, the ceiling tiles above her blurring as consciousness slipped. She recalls lying immobilised, lines running into both arms, a drip stand in her peripheral vision, unable to speak or call for her husband. It is precisely this helplessness — the body becoming a site of emergency rather than agency — that has made the aftermath so relentless.

The memories do not return to Aroha as recollections. When they come, she is back in the ICU bed: she feels the restraint of the sheets across her chest, the weight of her own limbs as they were then, heavy and unresponsive. The experience is fully sensory — the antiseptic smell, the beeping monitors, the fluorescent cold — and she cannot translate any of it into language. She has tried to explain it to her husband and found herself mute, gesturing helplessly at her sternum. This nonverbal, bodily quality of the memory is itself destabilising: because she cannot narrate what happened, she cannot distance herself from it, and the intrusions leave her convinced, in those moments, that her body is still failing. What frightened her most was not the illness itself but what the memories seemed to confirm — that her body had betrayed her without warning, that it could do so again at any moment, and that the life she had built was no longer structurally sound. She had come to believe that the trauma had destroyed something irreparable in her, and the shame she felt about what her body had become — scarred, monitored, dependent — sat beneath nearly everything else she reported.

These appraisals, in turn, have made the memories harder to escape. Because she understands what happened as evidence of permanent bodily unreliability, every intrusion feels confirmatory rather than historical, and she finds herself scanning her body constantly for new signals of failure. That vigilance keeps the traumatic material close to the surface, so that the memories recur more frequently and with greater force — and each recurrence deepens her certainty that she is not the person she was. The loop is self-sealing.

In her daily work as a project manager, Aroha now struggles to concentrate through meetings she once led with ease. She becomes irritable with colleagues over minor scheduling issues, and has twice reacted with visible alarm when a coworker touched her shoulder to get her attention — responses she finds humiliating and that reinforce her sense that her body is no longer her own. This state of chronic alertness is not passive: it feeds back into the traumatic memories themselves, so that a moment of startle or a flash of anger seems to summon the ICU back into her body. The threat state and the memories have become mutually sustaining.

Certain conversation topics — colleagues mentioning hospital stays, news items about cardiac events — are enough to trigger the full physiological alarm response, as is any medical context. A routine blood draw at her GP's office last spring, the sight of the needle and the drip stand in the corner of the room, sent her into a dissociative episode that lasted the remainder of the day. She has since cancelled two follow-up cardiology appointments. Her appraisals of her body as untrustworthy have made medical settings feel not like sites of safety but of renewed threat, and so the very care she needs has become something she avoids.

Aroha came to therapy at her husband's urging, after he found her sitting in the dark in their kitchen at 3 a.m., unable to explain why. She hopes, cautiously, to be able to return to her cardiologist. What she fears most is that she is right — that the person who walked into that hospital has not come back.
